B-47 nuclear bombers do a partial backflip called an "Immelman maneuver" and fling their nuclear weapons in a parabolic arc towards the target
Interesting. I knew about the maneuver, but I didn't think wide-bodies did it. I thought it was only for dive bombers and stuff.

The immelman is mostly for dogfighting, and always with an energy advantage. The typical case for it is an overshoot, you re-climb, and then do an immelman turn to reapproach (Whereas they have no chance of chasing you down because of your massive energy advantage allowing for you to climb way out of their reach). Additionally, they can't run away because your energy advantage allows you to turn altitude into speed. The other normal use case for it is if you're being chased and have an energy advantage, they should stall sooner than you and have to pull off (to avoid an overshoot below you and right into your gunsights). Doing an immelman turn allows you to do an air stall inversion or a low velocity loop, and turn the tables while retaining your energy advantage. Realistically, anything carrying a bomb payload would be really bad at it (bombs are heavy, and hinder climb rate quite badly), because they need a much bigger energy advantage to be able to use it meaningfully. Otherwise, they'll stall sooner than the pursuer and essentially come to a stop right in the pursuer's gunsights.

The application I read about was initially a trick some pilots used to bomb large targets with heavy anti-air defences, then later guidance computers were designed to automate the maneuver. In both cases they were smaller bombers, I'm rather surprised something the size of a b52 could do it at all without damaging itself/stalling.

You're not wrong. What you're referring to is called Toss Bombing and they do use an Immelman in one flavor of that (Over the shoulder). However, that's almost exclusively used with guided ammunitions (or things that are going to make a big enough explosion that it can't miss). The reason for that particular maneuver is to be low enough to avoid getting picked up on Radar prior to being in a position to deliver your payload, and then avoiding being anywhere near where the explosion is afterwards because of the way the force dynamics work (You're using centripetal force to loft the bomb a far distance away. Essentially, you're using the plane as a sling)
